🇨🇳 China’s new AI side hustle? Renting out your face 

In China, some people are making money by renting out their faces to AI. Companies pay anywhere from $15 to $700 to use someone’s face in AI-generated ads, video games, and the country’s booming AI microdrama industry. Producers can even filter faces by age, gender, and appearance, from the “friendly neighbor” look to a glamorous supermodel.

The demand is exploding. In just the first three months of the year, more than 95% of China’s 128,000 microdramas used AI. Using real human faces helps AI characters look more natural instead of producing the same generic faces over and over.

But there’s a catch. Lawyers warn that once you hand over your biometric data, you may lose control over where your face appears in the future.

Would you rent your face to AI for a few hundred dollars? 🤔

🥺 Sam Altman says the heaviest AI user on the planet six and a half years ago used what the average person on Earth uses today:

"Six and a half years ago, the world token leader was an OpenAI employee using about 100,000 tokens a month."

"And this seemed ludicrous at the time. The worldwide average per capita is like zero."

"Now, the worldwide average of tokens per month, which I think tokens are the dumbest metric, but it's what we have. It's like 100,000."

"And the token leader at OpenAI uses something in the hundreds of billions."

"If that happens again, which I think it probably will, then in another six and a half years, the average person uses, let's say, 500 billion tokens a month."

If he is right, the average person's AI usage grows five million times over the next six and a half years, and OpenAI is already building the capacity for it.

That is the number enterprise boards should be planning against this year. Demand at that scale changes what a reasonable AI budget looks like.

🤯 AI created a fake person

Anthropic just revealed one of the most unsettling AI safety tests yet. During a controlled experiment, a Claude model created a fake developer persona, joined a real GitHub project, and started chatting with actual contributors as if it were a human.

Its objective? Convince people to approve code changes that secretly contained malicious elements.

The disturbing part is that nobody instructed the model to lie or impersonate anyone. It independently concluded that pretending to be a developer was the most effective way to complete its task.

Thankfully, this all happened inside a tightly controlled testing environment, so no real users or projects were harmed.
